extracted.intended_audience: writers, screenwriters, students, and general readers interested in narrative/plot devices
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive criteria for creating and evaluating cliffhanger endings in serialized fiction, film, television, comics, and prose. Covers definition, purposes, forms, resolution methods, timing, ethical concerns, and media-specific conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: precarious situation / shocking revelation
rubrics_metrics.description: A cliffhanger (or cliffhanger ending) is a plot device in fiction which features a main character in a precarious situation, facing a difficult dilemma or confronted with a shocking revelation at the end of an episode of serialized fiction or before a commercial break in a television programme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the core identifying feature: ending an installment on a moment of unresolved danger, dilemma, or revelation. Applies across media (serial fiction, television, film, manga, comics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose: incentivize audience return / provoke thought
rubrics_metrics.description: A cliffhanger is intended to incentivize the audience to return to see how the characters resolve the dilemma, or to provide a mysterious or thought provoking ending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a cliffhanger when you want to increase anticipation, ensure audience retention between installments, or leave the reader thinking; the device's success is measured by whether it motivates return/viewing and sustains interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary forms: perilous suspense or sudden revelation
rubrics_metrics.description: The two main ways for cliffhangers to keep readers/viewers coming back is to either involve characters in a suspenseful, possibly life-threatening situation, or to feature a sudden shocking revelation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose between bodily/peril stakes (life-or-death, capture, imminent danger) and informational stakes (major reveal about identity/plot). Both can be effective; combine carefully to avoid melodrama or cheap shocks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolution (take-out) types for serials: sequential, augmented, incompatible
rubrics_metrics.description: Film serial take-outs (how the next installment resolves the cliffhanger) can be grouped into: sequential — continue the story by revealing facts or skipping to resolution; augmented — insert supplementary shots/scenes before the crisis; incompatible — present narrative information that directly conflicts with the original cliffhanger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be consistent and respect audience memory: sequential take-outs preserve continuity; augmented can fill gaps but risk feeling contrived if added only to patch plot holes; incompatible take-outs risk viewer distrust because they contradict what was shown and can be perceived as cheating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate context: serialized media and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Cliffhangers are especially common and effective in serialized media (serial films, television series, soap operas, manga, comics) and are often placed at the end of episodes, issues, or before commercial breaks; historically used in serial novels and film serials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider medium-specific expectations: readers of serialized works expect episodic hooks; in single, non-serialized works a cliffhanger can feel out of place unless intentionally ambiguous. Placement (end of episode, season finale, issue) influences scale of the hook.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial-break scripting requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial breaks can be a nuisance to script writers because some sort of incompleteness or minor cliffhanger should be provided before each to stop the viewer from changing channels during the commercial break.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For broadcast TV, provide small, compelling beats before each ad break (a question, reveal, or mini-dilemma). These should be resolvable quickly and not undermine larger story cohesion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic/production use: uncertainty about renewal and actor availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Cliffhangers are sometimes deliberately inserted by writers who are uncertain whether a new series or season will be commissioned; they can also leave open the possibility of a character being killed off due to the actor not continuing to play the role.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using a cliffhanger as a hedge is a pragmatic strategy but can frustrate audiences if the series is not renewed or if 'conclusions' are manufactured later; be transparent in tone or plan for contingency resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolution expectation & permanence (deliberate vs. unresolved)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cliffhangers can be deliberate and permanent (author intends ambiguity and no sequel) or they can remain unresolved due to cancellation; occasionally unresolved cliffhangers are later revisited and resolved in follow-ups or revivals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether the lack of resolution is an artistic choice (ambiguous ending) or a production contingency. If permanent, ensure thematic justification; if contingent, be aware of audience dissatisfaction from unresolved arcs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical / audience-appropriateness considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Cliffhangers can cause controversy when they involve graphic violence or frightening images that may be inappropriate for certain audiences (example: Doctor Who complaint about a drowning scene seen as too frightening for children).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider audience age, broadcast standards, and potential for causing distress; balance dramatic impact with responsibility, especially in media with child audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overuse, laziness, and narrative risk
rubrics_metrics.description: The cliffhanger has become a genre staple to such a degree that series writers no longer feel they have to be immediately resolved, or even referenced, when the next episode is shown, variously because the writer did not feel it was 'a strong enough opener' or 'couldn't be bothered'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying on cliffhangers as a lazy mechanism to generate interest; overuse can blunt emotional payoff and erode audience trust. Ensure each cliffhanger is narratively justified and followed by a satisfying or meaningful continuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequel-tease function: introduce the next antagonist or element
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes a film, book, or season will end with the defeat of the main villain before a second, evidently more powerful villain makes a brief appearance (becoming the villain of the next film).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to escalate stakes across installments, but take care that the tease feels earned and not merely a gimmick to force continuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media-specific convention: frequency and audience expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Cliffhangers are especially frequent in Japanese manga and anime and in comics due to serialized publication norms; American primetime TV used them less before 1980 but they became common for season-enders thereafter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect the conventions and expectations of your chosen medium and audience: genres with a serialization tradition expect strong episodic hooks, while other formats may demand subtler or fewer cliffhangers.
